metadata.description: Design, develop, and manage secure, scalable, highly available, cost-effective Google Cloud solutions. The exam assesses the ability to design cloud solution architecture and manage implementation.

question.title: Compute Platform Selection
question.scenario: A retail company is building a new checkout microservice that must auto-scale from zero during off-peak hours, handle stateless HTTP requests, and deploy container images without managing cluster infrastructure.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud compute platform best fits these requirements?

choices.choice: Cloud Run
Google Kubernetes Engine Standard mode with Cluster Autoscaler
Compute Engine managed instance groups
App Engine Standard environment

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the platform that runs containers, scales to zero automatically, and requires no node or cluster management from the team.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Run is purpose-built for stateless containerized workloads: it scales from zero to thousands of instances based on incoming requests and back to zero when idle, with no cluster nodes to manage or pay for at rest. GKE Standard requires ongoing cluster and node pool management and does not scale to zero without additional tooling like KEDA. Compute Engine MIGs manage VM instances, not containers natively, and scale-to-zero is not supported. App Engine Standard supports only specific language runtimes, not arbitrary container images.

ul.li: Cloud Run bills per 100ms of CPU and memory only while a request is being processed, making it effectively free during zero-traffic windows â€” unlike GKE or GCE which bill for idle nodes.
Cloud Run supports concurrency settings (up to 1000 simultaneous requests per instance), allowing a single instance to handle many requests in parallel, which reduces cold-start frequency.
For workloads that need containers but also require stateful TCP connections, scheduled jobs, or GPU access, GKE Autopilot is a closer alternative that still removes node management burden.

question.title: GKE Node Pool Design
question.scenario: A data processing team runs batch jobs on GKE that are fault-tolerant and can restart from checkpoints. They want to minimize compute costs while ensuring the production API pods always have guaranteed capacity.
question.question-text: Which GKE node pool configuration best meets both requirements simultaneously?

choices.choice: A single node pool using on-demand N2 VMs for all workloads
Two node pools: on-demand nodes for API pods and Spot VM nodes for batch jobs, with node selectors
Autopilot mode with no node pool configuration
A single Spot VM node pool shared by both workload types

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Separate the workloads by their tolerance for interruption, then match each group to the pricing tier that fits its reliability requirement.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Using two node pools lets each workload class use the VM pricing tier that matches its reliability needs. Spot VMs can be up to 91% cheaper than on-demand but can be preempted with a 25-second notice; fault-tolerant batch jobs that checkpoint their state absorb this gracefully. The production API pods are scheduled onto on-demand nodes via node selectors or taints/tolerations, guaranteeing they are never evicted. Option A wastes money by running interruptible batch jobs on expensive on-demand VMs. Option D risks preempting the production API pods. Option C (Autopilot) does not expose per-workload node pool configuration.

ul.li: GKE Spot VM node pools use the same Spot VM pricing as standalone Compute Engine Spot VMs (up to 91% discount) and integrate with the Cluster Autoscaler to automatically replace preempted nodes.
Taints and tolerations enforce workload-to-node-pool placement: taint the Spot pool with cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true:NoSchedule and add a matching toleration only to batch job pod specs.

GKE Autopilot mode selects Spot pricing at the pod level using cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true" in the pod's nodeSelector, which is an alternative approach that still separates workloads without manual node pool management.

question.title: Load Balancer Type Selection
question.scenario: A media company serves video content globally and needs a single anycast IP address, SSL termination, and the ability to route requests to different backend services based on URL path.
question.question-text: Which load balancer type should the architect choose?

choices.choice: Regional external TCP/UDP Network Load Balancer
Regional external Application Load Balancer
Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer
Global external Application Load Balancer (HTTP(S))

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Only one load balancer type offers a global anycast IP, Layer 7 URL-map routing, and SSL offload in a single product.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Global external Application Load Balancer uses Google's anycast network, providing a single IP address that routes users to the nearest healthy backend worldwide. Its URL map supports path-based and host-based routing to direct traffic to different backend services or buckets. SSL is terminated at Google's edge PoPs, minimizing connection latency. The regional TCP/UDP load balancer (option A) operates at Layer 4 with no HTTP awareness and no global anycast. The internal load balancer (option C) has no external IP. The regional Application LB (option D) uses a regional IP, not anycast, limiting it to one region.

ul.li: Google's Premium Tier network carries traffic from the user's nearest edge PoP to the backend over Google's private backbone, reducing latency versus Standard Tier which uses public internet routing after the first hop.
URL maps support advanced routing: header-based routing, weight-based traffic splitting for canary deployments, and redirect rules â€” all configured without application-level logic changes.
Cloud Armor WAF policies attach directly to the Global ALB backend service, providing DDoS protection and OWASP rule sets at the edge before traffic reaches any backend VM or Cloud Run instance.

question.title: Cloud Storage Class Selection
question.scenario: A genomics research firm stores raw sequencing data files that are accessed frequently during a 30-day analysis window, then must be retained for 7 years for regulatory compliance with almost no subsequent access.
question.question-text: Which combination of storage classes best minimizes cost across the full retention lifecycle?

choices.choice: Standard for the first 30 days, then Archive for the remaining 7 years
Nearline for all 7 years
Standard for all 7 years
Coldline for the first 30 days, then Archive for the remaining 7 years

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Match each phase's access frequency to the storage class whose minimum storage duration and retrieval cost fit that phase's actual usage pattern.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Standard class has no minimum storage duration and no retrieval fee, making it appropriate for the actively accessed 30-day analysis window. After analysis, the data is rarely (if ever) retrieved, so Archive class at ~$0.0012/GB/month â€” the cheapest GCP storage tier â€” is optimal for 7-year cold retention. Object Lifecycle Management policies automate the class transition on day 30 without manual intervention. Option B (Nearline) costs more than Archive and is optimized for monthly access, not annual. Option C wastes money storing cold data in Standard at 10Ã— Archive's price. Option D uses Coldline during the active period, incurring retrieval fees for frequent access.

ul.li: Archive class has a 365-day minimum storage duration; objects deleted or replaced before that trigger an early deletion charge, so it should only be used for data retained longer than one year.

Object Lifecycle Management rules can be set on a bucket to automatically change the storage class of objects older than N days using SetStorageClass actions with age conditions â€” no application code changes needed.

Retrieval costs: Standard $0/GB, Nearline $0.01/GB, Coldline $0.02/GB, Archive $0.05/GB â€” retrieval fees make Archive expensive for any data that is periodically retrieved, so access pattern must truly be near-zero.

question.title: Workload Identity Federation
question.scenario: An application running on an on-premises Kubernetes cluster needs to write data to a Cloud Storage bucket. The security team prohibits storing service account key files on any system.
question.question-text: Which authentication approach allows the on-premises workload to access GCP without long-lived key files?

choices.choice: Export a service account JSON key and mount it as a Kubernetes secret
Create a static HMAC key for the service account and store it in Secret Manager
Embed the service account key in the container image at build time
Use Workload Identity Federation to exchange the cluster's OIDC token for short-lived GCP credentials

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which mechanism lets an external identity provider issue tokens that GCP accepts, so no permanent GCP credentials ever leave Google's infrastructure.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Workload Identity Federation allows workloads running outside GCP to authenticate using tokens from an external identity provider (in this case, the on-premises Kubernetes cluster's OIDC issuer). GCP's Security Token Service exchanges the short-lived OIDC token for temporary GCP access tokens scoped to a specific service account â€” no JSON key files are ever created or stored. Options A and C both involve long-lived key files and violate the security team's policy; key files also cannot be automatically rotated. Option D stores an HMAC key (which is itself a long-lived credential) in Secret Manager, which still violates the no-key-file policy.

ul.li: Workload Identity Federation supports OIDC and SAML 2.0 providers; for Kubernetes clusters, the cluster's built-in service account token issuer is registered as a trusted pool in GCP IAM.

After federation, the external workload uses the gcloud CLI or client libraries with Application Default Credentials (ADC) pointing to a credentials configuration file that describes how to exchange tokens â€” this file contains no secrets.

Attribute conditions in the workload identity pool restrict which external identities can impersonate a given service account (e.g., only pods with a specific Kubernetes service account name in a specific namespace), enforcing least privilege across the trust boundary.

question.title: Shared VPC Design
question.scenario: A large enterprise runs separate GCP projects for development, staging, and production teams. The networking team needs centralized control over subnets and firewall rules while allowing each team's project to deploy VMs into those subnets.
question.question-text: Which networking model best achieves centralized network administration with project-level resource autonomy?

choices.choice: Create a separate VPC in each project and connect them with VPC peering
Use Cloud VPN to connect each project's VPC to a central hub VPC
Use Shared VPC with a host project owning the network and service projects consuming it
Deploy all resources in a single project with IAM folder-level separation

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which model lets one team own and control subnets while other teams deploy VMs into those same subnets from their own projects.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Shared VPC centralizes network resources (subnets, firewall rules, routes) in a host project while service projects attach to it and launch instances using the shared subnets. The networking team retains full control in the host project; individual teams deploy VMs in their service projects but cannot modify the subnets. VPC peering (option A) connects separate VPCs but each project still manages its own network; there is no central firewall control. Cloud VPN (option C) adds latency, complexity, and cost for cross-project communication and still doesn't unify firewall administration. Option D collapses all resources into one project, breaking billing and access isolation.

ul.li: Shared VPC requires the host project to be in the same organization. The roles/compute.networkUser role is granted to service project service accounts at the subnet level, enabling fine-grained subnet access control.

Firewall rules in the host project's VPC apply to all service projects' VMs simultaneously; a single firewall policy change by the network team propagates instantly across all attached service projects.

VPC peering, by contrast, is non-transitive: if project A peers with project B and B peers with project C, A cannot reach C through B â€” a hub-and-spoke with Shared VPC or Network Connectivity Center avoids this limitation.

question.title: BigQuery Partitioning Strategy
question.scenario: A marketing analytics team queries a BigQuery table containing 5 years of click-stream events (approximately 10 TB) and almost always filters on a date range within the past 90 days. Query costs are escalating due to full-table scans.
question.question-text: Which BigQuery optimization most directly reduces query cost for this access pattern?

choices.choice: Partition the table by event_date and require a partition filter in queries
Create a materialized view that pre-aggregates the full 5-year dataset
Cluster the table by user_id to reduce bytes scanned
Export the data to Cloud Storage and use BigQuery external tables

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When queries consistently filter on a time column, dividing the table into time-based segments means only the relevant segments are read and billed.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Date partitioning divides the table into daily (or monthly/yearly) segments stored separately. When a query includes a partition filter on the date column (e.g., WHERE event_date BETWEEN ...), BigQuery reads only matching partitions â€” for 90-day queries against 5 years of data, roughly 95% of bytes are pruned. Requiring a partition filter (partition pruning enforcement) prevents accidental full scans. Option B (materialized view) pre-aggregates but doesn't help ad-hoc queries at the row level. Option C (clustering) improves performance within a partition but does not reduce the partitions scanned; clustering is complementary, not a replacement. Option D adds unnecessary complexity and external table query performance is slower.

ul.li: BigQuery supports ingestion-time partitioning (automatic, on _PARTITIONTIME), column partitioning (on a DATE/TIMESTAMP/INTEGER column), and range partitioning; column partitioning on an explicit event_date is the most precise and transparent option.
Enabling require_partition_filter on the table prevents queries that do not include a partition filter from executing, eliminating accidental full-table scan billing.

Clustering on columns used in GROUP BY or additional WHERE filters (e.g., campaign_id) can be combined with partitioning; BigQuery uses clustering metadata to skip blocks within a partition, further reducing bytes billed beyond partition pruning alone.

question.title: Cloud SQL High Availability
question.scenario: A SaaS company runs its primary database on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL and needs to survive a zonal failure with minimal downtime and zero data loss. The application must reconnect automatically after failover.
question.question-text: Which Cloud SQL configuration achieves zero RPO and minimal RTO for a zonal failure?

choices.choice: Enable High Availability (regional) with an automatic failover replica in a different zone
Create a read replica in a second zone and promote it manually when the primary fails
Schedule hourly backups to Cloud Storage and restore from backup on failure
Use Cloud SQL with a single zone and rely on GCP's infrastructure SLA

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Which option uses synchronous replication so committed transactions are always present on the standby, and triggers failover automatically without operator intervention?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud SQL HA (regional configuration) provisions a standby instance in a different zone that receives synchronous writes â€” every committed transaction exists on both primary and standby before the application receives an acknowledgment, achieving zero RPO. Failover is automatic within 60 seconds and the connection endpoint (Cloud SQL proxy or public IP) remains the same, so the application reconnects without configuration changes. A manually promoted read replica (option B) uses asynchronous replication, so RPO is non-zero, and the manual step means RTO is human-dependent. Hourly backups (option C) can lose up to an hour of data. Single-zone (option D) has no protection against zonal failures.

ul.li: Cloud SQL HA uses a regional persistent disk that synchronously replicates at the storage layer; this means both primary and standby share the same underlying data, making the standby immediately ready with zero data divergence.

During failover, Cloud SQL promotes the standby instance and updates internal DNS within approximately 60 seconds; applications using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or private IP see a brief connection interruption but no endpoint change.

Read replicas are asynchronous and serve a different purpose â€” scale-out for read-heavy workloads, cross-region disaster recovery â€” but they do not provide zero RPO because replication lag can leave the replica behind the primary at the moment of failure.

question.title: Global Transactional Database
question.scenario: A fintech startup is building a payment processing system that must maintain strong consistency for account balances across users in North America, Europe, and Asia, with transactions spanning multiple rows and tables.
question.question-text: Which GCP database service is purpose-built for globally distributed, strongly consistent relational transactions?

choices.choice: Cloud SQL with cross-region read replicas
Cloud Spanner with a multi-region configuration
Firestore in Datastore mode with global replication
BigTable with a multi-cluster replication topology

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Only one GCP database provides external consistency (the strongest consistency model) combined with full SQL support and automatic, synchronous global replication.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner is the only relational database that provides external consistency (stronger than serializable isolation) across globally distributed regions. Its TrueTime API allows Spanner to assign globally meaningful timestamps, enabling multi-row, multi-table transactions that commit synchronously across regions. Cloud SQL (option B) uses asynchronous cross-region replication, meaning read replicas may lag and cannot participate in cross-region transactions. Firestore (option C) is a document database with eventual consistency across regions; it does not support relational multi-row ACID transactions. Bigtable (option D) is a NoSQL wide-column store without SQL or multi-row transactional semantics.

ul.li: Cloud Spanner's TrueTime uses GPS receivers and atomic clocks in Google's data centers to bound clock uncertainty; transactions are assigned commit timestamps that are guaranteed to reflect global ordering without coordination latency.

Multi-region Spanner configurations (e.g., nam-eur-asia1) place read-write replicas across three continents; a quorum write requires acknowledgment from a majority of replicas before committing, ensuring zero RPO during a regional outage.

Spanner supports the full ANSI SQL dialect with JOINs, subqueries, and DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), making it a drop-in conceptual replacement for large-scale PostgreSQL or MySQL deployments that have outgrown single-region limitations.

question.title: Event-Driven Pub/Sub Architecture
question.scenario: An IoT platform ingests sensor readings from 50,000 devices at unpredictable burst rates. Downstream analytics and alerting services must process events independently and at their own pace without the ingestion layer being coupled to consumer speed.
question.question-text: Which architectural component should decouple the sensor data ingestion layer from the downstream processing services?

choices.choice: Cloud Pub/Sub with separate subscriptions for each downstream consumer
Cloud Tasks queues with one task per sensor reading
Direct gRPC streaming from devices to each downstream service
Cloud Storage as a staging area with periodic polling by consumers

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which service was designed for fan-out message delivery where the same event is independently consumed by multiple subscribers at their own throughput.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Pub/Sub is built for exactly this pattern: publishers push messages to a topic and each subscription receives an independent copy, allowing analytics and alerting services to consume at their own rate without affecting each other or the ingestion path. Pub/Sub can handle millions of messages per second and automatically absorbs bursts without backpressure to the devices. Cloud Tasks (option B) is designed for task dispatch to a single handler with deduplication, not fan-out to multiple consumers. Direct gRPC (option C) couples devices to downstream services, meaning each new consumer requires changes to device firmware or the ingestion gateway. Polling Cloud Storage (option D) adds latency, does not scale elegantly for high-frequency events, and creates storage costs proportional to message volume.

ul.li: Pub/Sub subscriptions can be push (Pub/Sub calls an HTTP endpoint on the consumer) or pull (consumer polls Pub/Sub for messages); push subscriptions work well with Cloud Run while pull subscriptions integrate naturally with Dataflow streaming pipelines.

Dead-letter topics can be configured per subscription: after a configurable number of delivery attempts, unacknowledged messages are forwarded to a dead-letter topic for inspection, preventing stuck messages from blocking the subscription.

Pub/Sub Lite is a lower-cost, lower-latency alternative for high-throughput workloads where zonal availability (rather than global) is acceptable; it uses pre-provisioned capacity instead of auto-scaling, trading cost for predictability.

question.title: Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor
question.scenario: A news website serves global readers and has experienced volumetric DDoS attacks that saturated its origin servers. The team wants to cache static content at the edge and block malicious traffic before it reaches the origin.
question.question-text: Which combination of services should the architect deploy in front of the origin servers?

choices.choice: Cloud CDN alone to cache and absorb attack traffic
Cloud Armor alone with a DDoS protection policy
Cloud Armor with a regional Application Load Balancer and Cloud CDN disabled
Cloud CDN with Cloud Armor security policies attached to the Global Application Load Balancer backend service

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: CDN and WAF/DDoS protection serve complementary roles â€” one reduces origin load for legitimate traffic, the other filters malicious requests â€” and both attach to the same load balancer layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud CDN caches cacheable responses at Google's globally distributed edge PoPs, so the majority of legitimate user requests never reach the origin. Cloud Armor applies WAF rules and rate limiting at the same edge layer, blocking malicious requests before they consume origin resources. Both are configured on the Global Application Load Balancer backend service â€” Cloud CDN as a backend bucket/service cache setting and Cloud Armor as a security policy. CDN alone (option A) reduces origin load but does not block attackers who send uncacheable requests. Cloud Armor alone (option B) blocks threats but doesn't reduce origin load for legitimate traffic. Option D uses a regional LB which has no global anycast, negating edge-based protection.

ul.li: Cloud Armor's Adaptive Protection uses ML to detect volumetric DDoS attacks in real time and automatically suggests (or enforces, in auto-deploy mode) rate-based rules to block attacking source IPs at Google's edge before traffic enters the network.

Cloud CDN cache hit ratio can be monitored in Cloud Monitoring; a high cache hit ratio means most DDoS volume for cacheable resources is absorbed at the CDN layer without Cloud Armor even needing to evaluate rules for those requests.

Cloud Armor supports both pre-configured WAF rules (OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set) and custom rules using CEL expressions; rules can be scoped to specific paths, headers, or IP ranges, enabling surgical protection without broad blocking.

question.title: CI/CD with Cloud Build
question.scenario: A development team wants to automatically build a Docker image, run unit tests, push the image to a private registry, and deploy to Cloud Run every time code is merged to the main branch in their GitHub repository.
question.question-text: Which GCP services provide a fully managed CI/CD pipeline for this workflow?

choices.choice: Cloud Build triggered by GitHub push events, with Artifact Registry as the image store
Compute Engine VMs running Jenkins with Container Registry
Cloud Run jobs for build steps with Cloud Storage for image storage
Cloud Functions triggered by GitHub webhooks, building images inline

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the fully managed build service that natively integrates with GitHub triggers and the recommended GCP container registry service.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Build is a fully managed CI/CD platform that can be triggered by pushes to GitHub (or Cloud Source Repositories) via build triggers. A cloudbuild.yaml file defines steps: build the Docker image, run tests, push to Artifact Registry (the successor to Container Registry), and deploy to Cloud Run using the gcloud deploy step. Artifact Registry provides a managed, private Docker-compatible registry with vulnerability scanning and IAM-controlled access. Option B requires self-managing Jenkins on VMs and is not fully managed. Option C is not a standard build workflow; Cloud Run jobs are for running containerized workloads, not CI builds. Option D would hit Cloud Functions memory and timeout limits trying to run a Docker build.

ul.li: Cloud Build build triggers support GitHub, Bitbucket, and Cloud Source Repositories; they can filter on branch name, tag patterns, or changed file paths (e.g., only trigger when files under src/ change) to avoid unnecessary builds.

Artifact Registry supports multiple formats beyond Docker: Python packages (PyPI), Java artifacts (Maven/Gradle), npm packages, and Helm charts â€” making it a unified artifact store for polyglot repositories.

Cloud Build's built-in service account can be granted roles/run.admin and roles/iam.serviceAccountUser to deploy to Cloud Run directly from a build step, enabling zero-infrastructure CD without external orchestration tools.

question.title: Disaster Recovery RTO and RPO
question.scenario: A logistics company's order management system has an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 1 hour. The system runs on GCE instances with a PostgreSQL database and serves regional traffic only.
question.question-text: Which DR strategy is the most cost-effective way to meet these specific RTO and RPO targets?

choices.choice: Warm standby: replicated instances running at reduced capacity in a second region, ready to scale up
Active-active: full capacity in two regions simultaneously
Pilot light: minimal infrastructure in a second region, with hourly database backups restored on failover
Backup and restore: full environment backup daily, restored from scratch on failover

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Match the DR tier to the targets: the strategy needs to meet 4-hour RTO and 1-hour RPO without spending on a full always-on standby.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Pilot light keeps the minimum infrastructure (networking, load balancer, IAM) pre-configured in the DR region, with the application and database not running. Hourly Cloud SQL exports to Cloud Storage ensure RPO â‰¤ 1 hour. On failover, restoring a 1-hour-old backup and starting instances can be completed within 4 hours, meeting the RTO. This is the cheapest DR tier that still meets the stated targets. Warm standby (option A) meets the targets but costs more because instances are always running. Active-active (option B) exceeds requirements at much higher cost. Daily backup and restore (option D) cannot meet the 1-hour RPO requirement.

ul.li: The four DR tiers by cost ascending: backup-and-restore (highest data loss), pilot light (minimal infra pre-built), warm standby (reduced-capacity active), active-active (zero downtime) â€” choose the cheapest tier whose RTO/RPO still satisfy the SLA.

Cloud SQL supports automated backups with configurable frequency (up to every 1 hour for transaction log backups with point-in-time recovery), and exports to Cloud Storage can be scripted via Cloud Scheduler for the pilot light pattern.

Infrastructure as Code (Terraform or Deployment Manager) is essential to the pilot light pattern: the DR environment is defined in code and can be provisioned in minutes, but resource creation time must be factored into the RTO estimate.

question.title: Cloud Monitoring Alerting
question.scenario: An SRE team wants to receive a PagerDuty notification when the error rate on a Cloud Run service exceeds 1% of requests over a 5-minute window, and wants visibility into the historical trend before acknowledging an alert.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Monitoring features should the architect configure to implement this alerting and visibility requirement?

choices.choice: An alerting policy with a metric threshold condition on request_count filtered by response_code_class=5xx, a PagerDuty notification channel, and a linked dashboard
A Cloud Logging sink to BigQuery with a scheduled query that emails the team daily
Cloud Trace with latency percentile alerts sent to Cloud Pub/Sub
A Cloud Function triggered by log entries containing "ERROR" that calls PagerDuty's API

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which option uses native metric-based alerting with a built-in notification channel integration rather than requiring custom code or data pipeline delays.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Monitoring alerting policies evaluate metric time series against threshold conditions over configurable alignment periods (5 minutes in this case). The error rate can be computed as a ratio metric combining the 5xx request count against total request count. PagerDuty is a natively supported notification channel in Cloud Monitoring â€” no custom webhook code is needed. Linking a dashboard to the alerting policy lets responders see the historical trend directly from the alert notification. Option B is a delayed analytics approach, not real-time alerting. Option C is for latency tracing, not error rate monitoring. Option D requires writing and maintaining custom code and cannot filter by rate (percentage) without additional logic.

ul.li: Cloud Monitoring supports ratio conditions in alerting policies: you can define a condition where the numerator metric (5xx errors) divided by the denominator metric (all requests) must exceed a threshold, directly measuring error rate percentage without pre-processing.

Notification channels in Cloud Monitoring support PagerDuty, Slack, email, SMS, webhooks, and Pub/Sub; multiple channels can be attached to a single alerting policy so the team is notified on multiple surfaces simultaneously.

Alert policies can include documentation fields with runbook URLs, alert context, and playbook steps; this documentation appears in the PagerDuty incident description, reducing mean time to resolution for on-call engineers.

question.title: Anthos Hybrid Workloads
question.scenario: A manufacturing company runs mission-critical control systems on on-premises servers that cannot be migrated to the cloud due to latency requirements, but wants unified application management, consistent security policies, and cloud-based monitoring across both environments.
question.question-text: Which GCP product enables unified Kubernetes cluster management across on-premises and GCP environments?

choices.choice: GKE clusters in GCP managing on-premises VMs via SSH
Cloud Run with a VPN tunnel to on-premises servers
Anthos (GKE Enterprise) with Anthos Config Management and Cloud Monitoring
Migrate for Compute Engine replicating on-premises VMs to GCE

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the product designed explicitly for hybrid and multi-cloud Kubernetes fleet management with centralized policy enforcement.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Anthos (now branded GKE Enterprise) registers on-premises Kubernetes clusters (running on bare metal or VMware) and GKE clusters in GCP as a unified fleet. Anthos Config Management synchronizes policies, RBAC, and Kubernetes configurations from a Git repository across all clusters in the fleet, ensuring consistent security posture. Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging collect telemetry from all clusters centrally. The on-premises control systems remain local, satisfying the latency constraint. Cloud Run (option B) is fully managed serverless and cannot run on-premises. Option C describes manual VM management, not unified container orchestration. Migrate for Compute Engine (option D) physically moves workloads to GCP, which the scenario explicitly prohibits.

ul.li: Anthos clusters on bare metal use the Connect Agent to establish a secure outbound connection to Google's control plane over HTTPS, so no inbound firewall rules from GCP to the data center are required.

Anthos Config Management uses a GitOps model: a root sync points to a Git repository, and the config management operator on each cluster continuously reconciles live cluster state with the declared state in Git, automatically correcting drift.

Anthos Service Mesh (managed Istio) can be deployed across the fleet to provide mTLS between services, unified traffic management, and distributed tracing even for on-premises clusters â€” giving the same observability as pure-cloud deployments.

question.title: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys
question.scenario: A defense contractor must store sensitive project files in Cloud Storage and requires that they control the encryption keys. Regulatory requirements mandate that GCP employees cannot access the plaintext data even during support operations.
question.question-text: Which encryption configuration satisfies the requirement for customer-controlled keys with GCP employee access restrictions?

choices.choice: Google-managed encryption keys (default)
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) stored in Cloud KMS with Key Access Justifications enabled
Client-side encryption only, with keys stored locally and never uploaded to GCP
CMEK stored in Cloud KMS without any additional access logging

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which option places key custody in the customer's hands while also providing an audit trail for any internal Google access to the key material.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: CMEK allows the customer to create and manage encryption keys in Cloud KMS; GCP services encrypt data using these keys but the customer can revoke key access at any time, rendering the data inaccessible. Key Access Justifications is an add-on that requires Google to provide a machine-readable reason for every internal access to a key and allows the customer to automatically deny unjustified requests â€” this directly satisfies the requirement that GCP employees cannot access plaintext without customer approval. Default Google-managed keys (option A) give no customer control or visibility. Client-side-only encryption (option C) satisfies the requirement but makes GCP services like BigQuery and Dataflow unable to read the data for processing. Option D uses CMEK without Key Access Justifications, so GCP employee access is not restricted or auditable.

ul.li: Cloud KMS supports software keys (Cloud KMS standard), hardware-protected keys (Cloud HSM, FIPS 140-2 Level 3), and externally managed keys where the actual key material never leaves the customer's HSM (Cloud EKM â€” External Key Manager).

CMEK integration is available for most GCP storage and analytics services: Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Spanner, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, GKE secrets, and more â€” each service's documentation specifies where the CMEK key reference is configured.

Revoking a Cloud KMS key version does not immediately delete data â€” it prevents future decryption operations. This is useful for compliance scenarios where data must be made immediately inaccessible (crypto-erasure) without physically deleting storage objects.

question.title: Committed Use vs Sustained Use Discounts
question.scenario: A company runs a set of n1-standard-8 GCE instances continuously 24/7 for a database cluster. A second group of instances runs for development builds â€” typically 4-6 hours per day at unpredictable times. The team wants to minimize VM costs for both groups.
question.question-text: Which discount strategy should be applied to each group?

choices.choice: Spot VMs for both groups to maximize savings
Committed Use Discounts (1-year) for the always-on database instances; Sustained Use Discounts apply automatically for the dev instances
Sustained Use Discounts for both groups without any commitments
Committed Use Discounts for both groups to get maximum savings

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Commitments pay off only for predictable, continuous usage; automatic discounts are better for variable or partial-month workloads.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) offer up to 57% savings on N1 machine types in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment. They are cost-effective when usage is predictably high (the database cluster runs 24/7, so the commitment is fully utilized). Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs) apply automatically when an instance runs more than 25% of a month â€” at full month usage a SUD provides ~30% discount with no commitment required. Development instances running 4-6 hours/day (~17-25% of the month) may not trigger SUDs at all, but they cannot justify a CUD either since they run sporadically. Spot VMs (option B) would be inappropriate for the always-on database cluster because they can be preempted. Buying CUDs for dev instances (option D) wastes commitment if instances don't run all month.

ul.li: Resource-based CUDs commit to a specific amount of vCPU and memory in a region (not tied to a specific instance type), so the discount applies as long as the committed resource amount is consumed â€” useful for fleets that resize instance types over a year.

Spend-based CUDs commit to a minimum hourly spend on eligible services (Cloud SQL, Cloud Run) rather than specific resource amounts, which is useful when the resource configuration changes frequently.

SUDs are calculated per machine type family per region across a billing account; running multiple smaller instances in the same family can accumulate toward a higher SUD tier, making fleet-level visibility in Cloud Billing important for cost management.

question.title: Organizational Policy Constraints
question.scenario: A CISO wants to ensure that no GCP project in the organization can create a Cloud Storage bucket with public access, regardless of who creates the project or what IAM permissions they have.
question.question-text: Which GCP feature enforces this restriction across all current and future projects in the organization?

choices.choice: A Cloud Monitoring alert that triggers when a public bucket is created
Granting only project owners the permission to create buckets
A Cloud Function that periodically scans buckets and removes public ACLs
An Organization Policy constraint that enforces uniform bucket-level access and restricts public access on all projects

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Only a preventive control that is applied at the organization level and evaluated before resource creation can block public buckets regardless of who creates the project.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Organization Policy Service allows administrators to set constraints at the organization, folder, or project level that override IAM permissions and are evaluated by GCP services at resource creation/modification time. The constraint constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention enforces that no bucket in scope can be made publicly accessible â€” even if a project owner tries to set a public ACL, the API call is rejected. Monitoring alerts (option A) and periodic scanning (option C) are detective/reactive controls, not preventive; a public bucket could exist for minutes or hours before being remediated. IAM restrictions (option D) only limit who can create buckets, not what properties those buckets can have.

ul.li: Organization policies are inherited from parent resources by default; a constraint set at the organization node applies to all folders and projects unless a child node has an explicit override (and override permission can itself be restricted using the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations or custom deny policy).

Policy tags (formerly listPolicy) allow or deny specific values; boolean constraints like storage.publicAccessPrevention are simpler â€” they're either enforced or not, with no value list to maintain.

The gcloud org-policies set-policy command or Terraform google_org_policy_policy resource can apply constraints to an organization; using IaC for org policies ensures they are version-controlled and auditable through the same change management process as infrastructure.

question.title: Data Residency Compliance
question.scenario: A European financial institution must ensure that all customer data remains within the EU at all times. The team is deploying Cloud Storage buckets and BigQuery datasets and needs a durable technical control â€” not just a policy document.
question.question-text: Which GCP mechanism provides a technical enforcement of data residency requirements for storage resources?

choices.choice: Selecting EU regions during resource creation and relying on team training
Enabling Cloud Audit Logs and reviewing them monthly for non-EU resources
Using VPC Service Controls to block all data access from outside the EU
Applying the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations Organization Policy to restrict resource creation to EU regions only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the preventive control that makes it technically impossible to create a storage resource outside the approved geographic boundary, regardless of operator intent.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The constraints/gcp.resourceLocations Organization Policy constraint accepts an allowedValues list of location IDs (e.g., europe-west1, europe-west4, eu) and prevents any resource creation in locations outside the list. This is a preventive technical control that applies uniformly across all projects in the organization without requiring developer awareness. Option A relies on human behavior, which is not a durable technical control. VPC Service Controls (option C) restrict which network contexts can access data, but do not restrict where data is stored. Audit Logs (option D) are detective, not preventive â€” a non-EU resource would already exist before the monthly review catches it.

ul.li: The gcp.resourceLocations constraint uses location IDs at multiple granularities: specific zones (europe-west1-b), regions (europe-west1), multi-regions (eu), and continent groupings; selecting in:eu-locations as an allowed value group covers all current and future EU GCP regions automatically.

This constraint is evaluated by the GCP Resource Manager at resource creation and update time; any API call that would place or move a resource outside the allowed locations is rejected with a FAILED_PRECONDITION error.

For BigQuery specifically, dataset location is set at creation and cannot be changed â€” combining the org policy with BigQuery dataset creation automation ensures no dataset ever lands in a non-EU location, even during development or testing.

question.title: Secret Manager vs Environment Variables
question.scenario: A developer is building a Cloud Run service that requires a database password. A colleague suggests storing the password as an environment variable in the Cloud Run service configuration. The security team objects to this approach.
question.question-text: Why should Secret Manager be used instead, and how should the secret be accessed from Cloud Run?

choices.choice: Environment variables are not supported by Cloud Run; Secret Manager is the only option

Secret Manager provides versioning, audit logs, IAM-controlled access, and automatic rotation â€” the secret value can be mounted as a volume or injected at startup without appearing in deployment configs
Secret Manager encrypts the value while environment variables do not; both are otherwise equivalent
Environment variables should be used for simplicity; Secret Manager adds unnecessary latency

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about what happens when the Cloud Run service configuration is exported, logged, or viewed by a team member â€” where does the password appear?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Environment variables in Cloud Run service configurations are stored in plaintext in the service definition, which is visible to anyone with run.services.get permission, appears in deployment manifests, may be logged in CI/CD systems, and cannot be audited for access. Secret Manager stores secret values encrypted, provides fine-grained IAM access (individual service accounts are granted roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor), logs every access in Cloud Audit Logs, supports versioning and rotation, and Cloud Run can inject secrets directly at container startup as environment variables or file mounts â€” so the secret value never appears in the service configuration. Option A is false; Cloud Run supports env vars. Option C understates the difference. Option D's latency concern is negligible for startup-time secret fetching.

ul.li: Cloud Run's native Secret Manager integration injects secrets at container startup before the application starts; the secret value is fetched by the Cloud Run control plane using the service account's identity, so application code never needs to call the Secret Manager API or handle credentials to fetch credentials.

Secret versions allow zero-downtime rotation: create a new secret version, update the Cloud Run service to reference latest (or the new version), and deploy â€” the old version remains accessible for in-flight requests and can be disabled once the new revision is serving all traffic.

Cloud Audit Logs for Secret Manager record every AccessSecretVersion call with the caller's identity, timestamp, and secret name â€” providing the audit trail required by SOC 2 and similar compliance frameworks to demonstrate that secret access is monitored.

question.title: Cloud Functions vs Cloud Run
question.scenario: A team needs to build two serverless components: (1) a simple webhook handler that receives HTTP events from a third-party SaaS and writes to Firestore â€” expected execution under 5 seconds; and (2) a video transcoding service that processes uploaded files and may run for up to 45 minutes.
question.question-text: Which serverless platform is appropriate for each component?

choices.choice: Cloud Functions (2nd gen) for the webhook handler; Cloud Run for the video transcoding service
Cloud Functions (2nd gen) for both components
Cloud Run for both components
App Engine Standard for the webhook handler; Cloud Run for video transcoding

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Check the maximum execution timeout for each platform and match the long-running workload to the one with a higher limit.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Functions 2nd gen (backed by Cloud Run) has a maximum timeout of 60 minutes for HTTP functions, but the standard recommended use case is short-lived event handlers where the simplicity of a single function file is a benefit. The webhook handler is a perfect fit: it's short-lived, event-driven, and benefits from Cloud Functions' simplified deployment model. Cloud Run supports request timeouts up to 60 minutes for HTTP requests and is the appropriate choice for the video transcoder, which may need 45 minutes and likely requires a custom Docker image with ffmpeg or similar. While Cloud Functions 2nd gen technically has a 60-minute limit, Cloud Run provides the container flexibility needed for a video processing workload with custom binaries. Option A misuses Cloud Functions for a workload that needs custom container control. Option D brings App Engine without justification.

ul.li: Cloud Functions 2nd gen is actually built on Cloud Run internally, meaning it inherits Cloud Run's per-instance concurrency model; however, Cloud Functions abstracts away the Dockerfile and container build, making it simpler for teams deploying single-purpose event handlers.

Cloud Run Jobs (as opposed to Cloud Run services) are designed for long-running batch tasks without an HTTP endpoint; for video transcoding triggered by Cloud Storage events, Cloud Run Jobs with Eventarc integration may be more appropriate than an HTTP service.

Memory limits differ: Cloud Functions 2nd gen supports up to 32 GB RAM and 8 vCPUs per instance, which may be sufficient for in-memory video processing, but Cloud Run allows more granular container specification for workloads with specific CPU/memory ratios.

question.title: Cloud Interconnect vs Cloud VPN
question.scenario: A bank's on-premises data center needs a private connection to GCP for daily batch transfers of 5 TB of transaction records. Compliance requires that data not traverse the public internet. The team is evaluating latency and bandwidth requirements for a dedicated connection.
question.question-text: Which hybrid connectivity option is most appropriate for this high-bandwidth, compliance-driven use case?

choices.choice: Dedicated Interconnect providing a private, high-bandwidth physical connection to Google's network
Cloud VPN with HA VPN over the public internet with AES-256 encryption
Cloud VPN with a single tunnel and static routing
Public internet with TLS encryption and client-side VPN software

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When compliance requires private connectivity (not just encrypted traffic over public networks), and bandwidth requirements are in the tens of gigabits, only a physical circuit meets both requirements.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Dedicated Interconnect provides a private Layer 2 physical circuit between the customer's data center and a Google colocation facility, with no traffic traversing the public internet. It supports 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps circuits and can be bundled into larger bundles (up to 800 Gbps). Transferring 5 TB daily comfortably at 10 Gbps takes roughly 70 minutes, well within a batch window. Compliance teams typically interpret "data must not traverse the public internet" as requiring physical private circuits, not just encryption over the internet. Cloud VPN (options A and C) routes traffic over the public internet even though it is encrypted â€” some compliance frameworks do not accept this. Option D is explicitly public internet and does not meet the stated requirement.

ul.li: Dedicated Interconnect requires a colocation presence near a Google POP; if the data center cannot co-locate, Partner Interconnect uses a service provider's network to extend connectivity from the provider's colocation to the customer site, still keeping traffic off the public internet.

HA VPN over Dedicated Interconnect is a design pattern where IPSec tunnels run over private Interconnect circuits to provide an additional encryption layer â€” used in high-security environments that require both private transport and application-level encryption.

Cloud Interconnect connections are billed per port (per-hour) plus per-GB egress to GCP (ingress from GCP to on-premises is free); for large daily transfers, the egress cost advantage of Interconnect over standard internet egress pricing can justify the port cost within months.

question.title: Binary Authorization Container Security
question.scenario: A financial services company's security policy requires that only container images that have passed a vulnerability scan and been approved by a security reviewer can be deployed to their GKE production cluster. Ad-hoc deployments of unscanned images must be blocked.
question.question-text: Which GCP feature enforces this supply-chain policy at deploy time on GKE?

choices.choice: Container Analysis API scanning integrated into Cloud Build, with results stored in Artifact Registry
Binary Authorization with an attestation policy that requires a signed attestation from the security scanner and reviewer before deployment
GKE admission webhook calling a custom Cloud Function to check image tags
Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning reports reviewed weekly by the security team

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The requirement is to block deployments at the Kubernetes admission layer â€” look for the GCP service that acts as an admission controller requiring cryptographic proof of approval before a pod can be created.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Binary Authorization is a deploy-time security control that integrates with GKE as an admission controller. It requires that container images presented for deployment carry cryptographic attestations signed by authorized attestors. In this case, the CI/CD pipeline would create an attestation after the vulnerability scan passes, and the security reviewer would create a second attestation after approval. The Binary Authorization policy on the cluster requires both attestations â€” unsigned or unattestation images are rejected before any pod is created. Container Analysis (option A) performs the scan but does not block deployments on its own. A custom admission webhook (option C1) requires writing and maintaining custom code. Weekly reviews (option C2) are detective, not preventive, and too slow to block ad-hoc deployments.

ul.li: Binary Authorization attestations are cryptographic signatures created using Cloud KMS asymmetric keys; the attestor's public key is registered in the Binary Authorization policy, and the GKE admission controller verifies the signature against the image digest at deploy time.

Binary Authorization policies support multiple modes: ALWAYS_ALLOW (audit only), ALWAYS_DENY, and REQUIRE_ATTESTATION; the policy can also define per-cluster or per-namespace overrides, allowing break-glass procedures with full audit trail.

The complete supply-chain security pipeline combines Container Analysis (vulnerability scanning), SLSA provenance generation in Cloud Build, Binary Authorization attestations, and Artifact Registry as the image registry â€” each layer provides defense-in-depth against supply-chain attacks.

question.title: SLOs and Error Budgets
question.scenario: An SRE team has defined a 99.9% availability SLO for an API. Over the past 30 days, the service experienced 65 minutes of downtime. The team is debating whether they can safely proceed with a risky infrastructure change this week.
question.question-text: Based on SRE principles, how should the team use the error budget to inform this decision?

choices.choice: Proceed with the change because the service has been running well for 30 days
Lower the SLO to 99.5% to create more error budget before proceeding
Immediately freeze all deployments and changes until the SLO reaches 100%
Calculate the remaining error budget: 99.9% SLO allows 43.8 minutes/month of downtime; the budget is exhausted and the risky change should be postponed until the budget resets

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Calculate how many minutes of downtime a 99.9% SLO allows per 30-day period, compare against actual downtime, and then apply the SRE principle for what to do when the error budget is depleted.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A 99.9% SLO allows 0.1% error rate over a 30-day window. 30 days Ã— 24 hours Ã— 60 minutes = 43,200 minutes Ã— 0.001 = 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime. The service has already experienced 65 minutes â€” the error budget is exhausted (by more than 20 minutes). SRE practice dictates that when the error budget is gone, reliability work takes priority over new feature releases or risky changes. The team should halt the risky change until the budget resets. Option A ignores the quantitative budget. Option C is too absolute â€” error budgets allow measured risk, not a freeze at 100%. Option D is a governance decision that should require stakeholder agreement, not a tactical workaround to enable a risky change.

ul.li: Error budget = (1 - SLO) Ã— time window; for 99.9% over 30 days: 0.001 Ã— 43,200 minutes = 43.2 minutes. The 65-minute actual downtime left the team 21.8 minutes over budget, meaning the SLO was missed this month.

Cloud Monitoring supports SLO monitoring natively: define a request-based or window-based SLO, and Cloud Monitoring calculates the error rate, remaining budget, and burn rate in real time â€” burn rate alerts fire when the budget is being consumed faster than the allowed rate.

Burn rate alerts are more actionable than threshold alerts: a 14.4Ã— burn rate means the monthly error budget will be exhausted in 2 hours, enabling the team to respond before users notice a sustained outage rather than reacting after the budget is already gone.

question.title: Lift-and-Shift VM Migration
question.scenario: An enterprise is migrating 200 on-premises Windows Server VMs to GCP with minimal changes to the operating system, applications, or data. The migration must minimize downtime and allow for a test cutover before the production cutover.
question.question-text: Which GCP service is designed for lift-and-shift VM migration with continuous replication and test clone capability?

choices.choice: Cloud Storage Transfer Service to copy VM disk images, then manually create GCE instances
Migrate for Compute Engine (formerly Velostrata) with continuous block-level replication to GCE
Database Migration Service configured for VM workloads
Anthos on bare metal to containerize each Windows VM during migration

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the GCP service specifically designed for migrating virtual machines in-place, with features for continuous replication and non-disruptive test cutovers.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Migrate for Compute Engine (formerly Velostrata, now part of the Migrate to Virtual Machines product family) performs continuous block-level replication of on-premises VMs to GCE while the source VM remains running. Once replication reaches near-zero delta, the team can initiate a test clone â€” a full copy in GCP that can be powered on to validate application behavior â€” without interrupting the source system. When the test passes, the production cutover is a brief maintenance window of minutes rather than hours. Cloud Storage Transfer (option B) copies files, not VM block devices, requiring manual VM reconstruction. Database Migration Service (option C) is for database workloads (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle), not general VMs. Anthos containerization (option D) is a refactoring effort, not a lift-and-shift migration.

ul.li: Migrate for Compute Engine uses a lightweight appliance installed in the on-premises environment to stream changed disk blocks to GCP over an HTTPS connection; the appliance can be deployed as a VM on VMware, Hyper-V, or AWS environments, supporting multi-source migrations.

The test clone feature creates an independent GCE instance from the current replication state; network access is isolated by default so the clone cannot accidentally communicate with production systems on-premises or in GCP during testing.

The Migration Center in GCP Console provides a unified view for discovery, dependency mapping, right-sizing recommendations (using collected utilization data), and wave planning to sequence the migration of interdependent VM groups, reducing the risk of breaking application dependencies during cutover.

question.title: Dataflow Pipeline Selection
question.scenario: A media analytics team ingests millions of clickstream events per second from a web platform. They need a unified pipeline that can handle both real-time dashboards and nightly batch reprocessing of historical data with identical transformation logic.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service and programming model best satisfies both the streaming and batch requirements with a single code path?

choices.choice: Cloud Dataflow with the Apache Beam SDK using a unified pipeline that runs in both streaming and batch modes
Separate Cloud Dataproc Spark Streaming jobs for real-time and Spark batch jobs for nightly reprocessing
Cloud Functions triggered by Pub/Sub for streaming, and BigQuery scheduled queries for batch
Kafka Streams on GKE for streaming and Apache Hive on Dataproc for batch

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the GCP service that is specifically designed around a unified batch/streaming programming model, eliminating duplicate transformation logic.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Dataflow is Google's fully managed execution environment for Apache Beam pipelines, which natively supports both bounded (batch) and unbounded (streaming) data sources through a single, portable SDK. The same pipeline code can run against Pub/Sub for real-time processing and against Cloud Storage or BigQuery for historical reprocessing simply by changing the runner configuration. Option B requires maintaining two separate codebases in different APIs. Option C splits logic across two unrelated services, making consistency harder to maintain. Option D introduces self-managed open-source infrastructure that defeats the managed-service goal.

ul.li: Apache Beam's windowing and triggering model (fixed, sliding, session windows) applies identically in streaming mode (Pub/Sub source) and batch mode (GCS/BigQuery source), making reprocessing semantically consistent with live processing.
Dataflow Streaming Engine offloads window state and shuffle to Google-managed infrastructure, enabling auto-scaling down to zero during quiet periods without managing worker pools.
Dataflow Flex Templates package pipeline code in containers, enabling version-controlled, repeatable launches via Cloud Scheduler or Cloud Workflows for nightly batch runs.

For exam scenarios, if the requirement is "unified batch and streaming with managed infrastructure," Dataflow/Beam is the canonical GCP answer; Dataproc is preferred when existing Spark or Hadoop code migration is the primary driver.

question.title: Event-Driven Service Routing
question.scenario: A DevOps team wants Cloud Build completion events to automatically trigger a Cloud Run service that updates a deployment dashboard, and Cloud Storage finalize events to trigger a separate data validation functionâ€”all without writing custom polling code.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service should the team use to route these events from GCP sources to their target services?

choices.choice: Cloud Tasks queues populated by a central Cloud Function that polls all GCP APIs every 30 seconds
Cloud Pub/Sub with custom subscriber code in each target service that polls for its specific event type
Cloud Scheduler calling each target service endpoint on a one-minute cron interval
Eventarc, configuring triggers that listen to Cloud Audit Logs and direct GCP event sources and routing events to Cloud Run or Cloud Functions targets

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Identify the GCP service purpose-built to route events from first-party GCP event sources to serverless targets without custom polling or fan-out logic.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Eventarc is Google Cloud's managed event routing service that delivers events from over 90 GCP sourcesâ€”including Cloud Build, Cloud Storage, and Cloud Audit Log entriesâ€”directly to Cloud Run services, Cloud Functions (2nd gen), and GKE workloads using CloudEvents format. It removes the need to write subscriber polling code or manage Pub/Sub subscriptions manually. Option B works but requires each service to implement its own filtering logic, adding boilerplate. Option C uses polling intervals that introduce latency and waste compute when no events occur. Option D compounds the polling problem with a central bottleneck function.

ul.li: Eventarc triggers fall into two categories: direct triggers for services that natively emit CloudEvents (e.g., Cloud Storage, Firebase), and Cloud Audit Log triggers for any GCP API action that writes to audit logs, which covers nearly all GCP services.
Events are delivered in CloudEvents v1.0 format over HTTPS to the target service's root path, making handlers portable across event sources and compliant with the CNCF standard.
Eventarc uses Pub/Sub internally for transport and inherits its at-least-once delivery guarantee; idempotent handlers are therefore a best practice for all Eventarc targets.

For exam questions, prefer Eventarc when routing GCP-native events to serverless targets; prefer raw Pub/Sub when the event source is application-generated or when fine-grained subscription management is needed.

question.title: In-Memory Caching Layer
question.scenario: An e-commerce application on GCP experiences high database read latency during flash sales. The team wants to add a managed in-memory caching layer within their VPC to cache session data and product catalog reads, reducing Cloud SQL query volume by 80%.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides a fully managed, VPC-native in-memory cache compatible with both Redis and Memcached protocols?

choices.choice: A self-managed Redis Cluster deployed on Compute Engine instances behind an internal load balancer
Cloud Bigtable with in-memory row caching enabled at the cluster level
Cloud Memorystore, choosing either the Redis or Memcached tier based on whether persistence and data structures are required
Cloud Spanner with stale reads configured to serve cached results from local replicas

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP has a fully managed service specifically designed for Redis and Memcachedâ€”no cluster management, no patching, no infrastructure to operate.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Memorystore is Google's fully managed in-memory data store service that supports Redis and Memcached. It provisions instances within the customer's VPC using Private Service Access, eliminating network traversal. For session data that benefits from persistence and richer data structures (sorted sets, hashes), Memorystore for Redis is appropriate; for simple key-value caching without persistence needs, Memcached offers higher throughput. Option B confuses Bigtable's purposeâ€”it is a wide-column store, not an in-memory cache. Option C introduces operational overhead that Memorystore eliminates. Option D uses Spanner stale reads for read scalability, not in-memory caching semantics.

ul.li: Memorystore for Redis supports versions 6.x and 7.x, and the Standard Tier provides a read replica and automatic failover with a 99.9% SLA, making it suitable for session-critical workloads.
Memorystore for Redis Cluster (GA as of 2024) supports horizontal sharding across up to 250 shards, delivering millions of QPS for workloads that outgrow a single Redis instance.
Memorystore instances are accessed only via internal IP within the VPC (or via VPC peering), so no firewall rules opening external ports are requiredâ€”an important security property.
For the exam, differentiate: Memorystore = managed Redis/Memcached; Firestore = document store; Bigtable = wide-column analytical/time-series; none of the others are in-memory caches.

question.title: GKE Pod IAM Identity
question.scenario: A Kubernetes application running on GKE needs to read objects from a Cloud Storage bucket. The security team prohibits storing service account key files in containers or Kubernetes Secrets, and requires that each pod use the minimum required GCP permissions.
question.question-text: Which mechanism allows GKE pods to authenticate to GCP APIs using IAM without managing service account keys?

choices.choice: Using the GKE node's Compute Engine service account to grant all pods on the node access to Cloud Storage
Mounting a JSON service account key as a Kubernetes Secret and setting GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS in the pod spec
GKE Workload Identity, which maps a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a GCP IAM service account and provides short-lived tokens via the metadata server
Creating a Cloud Storage signed URL generator Cloud Function that pods call to request temporary access

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The solution eliminates long-lived key files by bridging Kubernetes identity to GCP IAM using a federated token exchange at the node metadata server.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: GKE Workload Identity binds a Kubernetes ServiceAccount (KSA) in a specific namespace to a GCP IAM service account (GSA) using an annotation and an IAM binding. When a pod runs with that KSA, the GKE metadata server intercepts calls to the instance metadata endpoint and returns short-lived, automatically rotated tokens scoped to the bound GSA. No key files are created or stored. Option B violates the no-key-files requirement and creates a long-lived credential rotation problem. Option C violates least-privilege because all pods on the node share the same permissions. Option D adds unnecessary complexity and a dependency on a separate service.

ul.li: Workload Identity is enabled at the GKE cluster level with --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog; node pools must also enable the metadata server with --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA.

The binding is a two-part configuration: annotate the KSA with the GSA email, and grant the GSA the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role on the member serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA].

Workload Identity Federation (distinct from Workload Identity) extends the same keyless approach to workloads outside GKE (e.g., AWS EKS, GitHub Actions), using OIDC token exchange against the Security Token Service.
For GKE Autopilot clusters, Workload Identity is enabled by default and cannot be disabled, reinforcing it as the only supported pod-to-GCP authentication method in Autopilot.

question.title: Private Instance Outbound Access
question.scenario: A financial services company runs Compute Engine VMs with no external IP addresses for compliance. The VMs need to download software patches and reach third-party API endpoints on the internet, but inbound connections from the internet must be blocked.
question.question-text: Which GCP service enables outbound internet connectivity for VMs that have no external IP addresses without requiring each VM to have a public IP?

choices.choice: VPC Peering with a partner network that has direct internet egress
A bastion host VM with an external IP that all private VMs route through using a custom static route
Cloud NAT, configured on the subnet's Cloud Router to provide outbound-only SNAT for private VM traffic
Private Google Access, which allows VMs without external IPs to reach all internet destinations

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The purpose-built GCP service for outbound-only SNAT from private instances is a managed, scalable gateway that requires no VM-level configuration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud NAT is a fully managed, distributed network address translation service that allows VMs without external IPs to initiate outbound TCP/UDP connections to the internet. It is statefulâ€”only connections initiated from inside are allowed; inbound connections from the internet are blocked by design, satisfying the compliance requirement. Cloud NAT scales automatically and requires no single-point-of-failure NAT VM. Option B introduces a single-point-of-failure and operational burden. Option C requires a peering partner with internet access, which is an unusual and complex arrangement. Option D is incorrect: Private Google Access only allows VMs without external IPs to reach Google APIs and services (e.g., googleapis.com), not arbitrary internet endpoints.

ul.li: Cloud NAT is configured on a Cloud Router per region per VPC; it can cover all subnets, specific subnets, or specific VMs, giving fine-grained control over which resources get outbound internet access.
NAT IP addresses can be manually assigned (static) for scenarios where the third-party API requires IP allowlisting, or auto-allocated from Google's pool for dynamic scaling.
Cloud NAT logs (via Cloud Logging) capture translation events and can be filtered by source IP, destination IP, and port for compliance evidence of outbound traffic.
Distinguish for the exam: Private Google Access = reach google.googleapis.com endpoints; Cloud NAT = reach any internet destination; neither allows inbound connections from the internet.

question.title: GCS Data Retention and Versioning
question.scenario: A healthcare organization must retain medical imaging files for a minimum of seven years for regulatory compliance, automatically transition older files to cheaper storage classes, and recover accidentally deleted files within a 30-day window.
question.question-text: Which combination of Cloud Storage features satisfies all three requirements?

choices.choice: A Cloud Scheduler job that copies files to Coldline and deletes originals after 90 days, with no versioning
Object versioning to retain deleted-object versions, lifecycle policies to transition objects through storage classes, and a retention policy with a seven-year minimum retention period
WORM lock via a bucket-level ACL and manual archival to Nearline after one year
Object versioning only, with no lifecycle policy, relying on manual deletion audits

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Three distinct requirements map to three distinct Cloud Storage featuresâ€”look for the answer that activates all three rather than relying on manual or cron-based processes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Storage addresses all three requirements natively. Object versioning preserves non-current versions when objects are overwritten or deleted, enabling recovery within the 30-day window by restoring the most recent non-current version. Lifecycle policies automate transitions between storage classes (Standard â†’ Nearline â†’ Coldline â†’ Archive) based on object age, reducing cost without custom scripting. A bucket retention policy with a seven-year minimum prevents deletion or replacement of objects before the policy period expires, satisfying the regulatory hold. Option B relies on a fragile cron script with no deletion protection. Option C's ACL-based WORM is not a standard GCS featureâ€”retention policies are. Option D lacks the automated cost optimization and retention enforcement.

ul.li: Bucket retention policies are enforced at the API level; even project owners and the bucket owner cannot delete objects before the retention period expires unless the policy is first removedâ€”and removing it requires the lock to not be set.
Object lifecycle rules can filter by storage class, age, number of newer versions, and custom time metadata, enabling fine-grained automated tiering without code.

Soft delete (preview/GA by 2025) adds a bucket-level recycle bin that retains deleted objects for a configurable period (7â€“90 days) independently of versioning, providing an additional recovery path.
For compliance use cases, combine a locked retention policy (immutable) with Object Lock in compliance mode to satisfy SEC 17a-4 and similar regulations requiring WORM storage.

question.title: Budget Alerts and Spend Controls
question.scenario: A startup's development team has a $2,000 monthly GCP budget. The engineering manager wants to receive an email alert at 50% and 90% of the budget, and wants Cloud Run services to be automatically disabled if spend reaches 100% before month end.
question.question-text: Which GCP tooling correctly implements both the alerting and the automatic spend-capping requirements?

choices.choice: Cloud Monitoring alert policies on the billing/monthly_cost metric with email notification channels at 50% and 90%
Cloud Billing budgets with alert threshold rules at 50% and 90%, and a Pub/Sub-triggered Cloud Function that disables Cloud Run services when the 100% threshold notification arrives
A Cloud Scheduler job that queries the Billing Export BigQuery table every hour and sends email via SendGrid if spend exceeds the threshold
Organization Policy constraints that cap resource creation once estimated costs exceed the budget, with email alerts sent by the billing console automatically

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Billing budgets natively support threshold alerts; automated spend enforcement requires wiring the budget's Pub/Sub notification to a programmatic action.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Billing budgets allow you to set a dollar amount and configure multiple threshold rules (e.g., 50%, 90%, 100% of budget) that send email notifications to billing administrators and optionally publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Function subscribed to that topic can call the Cloud Run Admin API to update services to zero max-instances or disable traffic, effectively capping spend at 100%. Option B is incorrect because Cloud Monitoring does not expose a billing/monthly_cost metric for alerting in this way. Option C uses BigQuery billing export, which can have up to 24-hour lag, making it unsuitable for real-time spend control. Option D describes Organization Policy, which controls resource types, not spend amounts.

ul.li: Budget alerts fire based on actual spend or forecasted spend; the 100% actual threshold fires as soon as billing data is processed, typically within hours of cost accrual.

The Pub/Sub notification payload includes the budget name, project, currency amount, and the threshold rule that triggered, allowing the Cloud Function to apply project-specific or service-specific remediation logic.

Billing export to BigQuery (Standard Export and Detailed Export) provides a complete cost record but with a processing delayâ€”it is the right tool for analysis and dashboards, not real-time spend control.

Programmatic spend caps are a manual engineering responsibility in GCP; there is no native "hard cap" that halts all billing automaticallyâ€”the Pub/Sub + Cloud Function pattern is the recommended architecture for automated enforcement.

question.title: Multi-Tenancy with Cloud Identity
question.scenario: A SaaS company serves 200 enterprise customers, each requiring isolated GCP projects, separate identity management, and the ability for customers to use their own Google Workspace or Azure AD identities when accessing GCP resources. Customer administrators must not be able to access other tenants' resources.
