question.question-text: Which architecture correctly provides per-tenant identity isolation on Google Cloud?

choices.choice: A single Cloud Identity organization with per-customer folders and IAM policies binding each customer's Google Workspace or federated identities to only their folder's projects
One GCP project per customer sharing a single Cloud Identity domain, with IAM conditions restricting access by resource labels
Separate GCP organizations for each of the 200 customers, each with its own billing account managed by the SaaS company
Customer identities stored in a shared Cloud SQL database with a custom application layer enforcing access control outside of GCP IAM

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The key insight is that GCP's resource hierarchyâ€”organization, folders, projectsâ€”combined with IAM inheritance provides strong tenant isolation without requiring separate organizations.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A single Cloud Identity organization with per-customer folders is the recommended multi-tenancy pattern. Each customer's Google Workspace domain or federated external identities (via Workforce Identity Federation) are bound to IAM policies at their dedicated folder, and IAM inheritance ensures permissions do not cross folder boundaries. This keeps billing, audit logs, and policy management centralized for the SaaS provider while providing hard security isolation for tenants. Option B uses label-based IAM conditions, which are not a robust isolation boundary and are error-prone at 200 customers. Option C creates 200 separate organizations, which is operationally unmanageable and not how Google recommends multi-tenancy. Option D moves access control outside GCP IAM, losing audit trails and compliance properties.

ul.li: Workforce Identity Federation allows external IdP users (Azure AD, Okta, SAML 2.0, OIDC) to authenticate to GCP without creating Cloud Identity accounts, and attribute conditions in the pool configuration can restrict which external users can assume which roles.

Folder-level IAM policies are inherited by all projects and resources within the folder; combining folder IAM with Organization Policy constraints (e.g., allowed resource regions, allowed images) enforces per-tenant governance.
VPC Service Controls perimeters can be scoped per folder or per project, adding an API-level data exfiltration boundary on top of IAM for highly regulated tenants.
Audit logs are aggregated at the organization level via log sinks, enabling centralized SIEM ingestion while preserving per-tenant log isolation within their projects.

question.title: Progressive Delivery with Cloud Deploy
question.scenario: A retail company deploys a critical checkout service to GKE. The release engineering team wants to automatically roll out new versions to 10% of traffic first, monitor error rates for five minutes, and promote to 100% only if error rates stay below 1%â€”without writing custom CI/CD pipeline scripts.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service natively supports this canary delivery workflow with automated promotion gates?

choices.choice: Cloud Deploy with a delivery pipeline that defines canary phases, automated rollout rules, and verification steps that query Cloud Monitoring metrics before promotion
Cloud Build with a custom deployment step that uses kubectl to update Deployment replica counts and a shell script that polls error rates
GKE rolling update strategy with maxSurge and maxUnavailable set to control rollout speed
Artifact Registry release channels that automatically promote container images based on vulnerability scan results

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: One GCP service is purpose-built for progressive delivery with named pipeline stages, promotion gates, and metric-based verificationâ€”search for the managed CD service.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Deploy is Google Cloud's managed continuous delivery service for GKE, Cloud Run, and Anthos. It defines delivery pipelines with ordered stages (e.g., canary â†’ stable), supports canary deployments that split traffic using GKE Gateway or Istio, and includes verification steps that can query Cloud Monitoring metrics or run Cloud Build verification jobs before automatically or manually promoting to the next stage. If the error rate threshold is exceeded, the rollout can be automatically rolled back. Option B is a custom implementation that Cloud Deploy is designed to replace. Option C only controls update speed within a single Deployment, not traffic splitting. Option D describes Artifact Registry image management, not deployment orchestration.

ul.li: Cloud Deploy canary deployments integrate with GKE Gateway API or Anthos Service Mesh to split traffic at the load balancer or service mesh level, not by running duplicate Deployment objects.

Automated rollout rules in Cloud Deploy allow defining advance conditions (e.g., "if Cloud Monitoring query returns error rate below 1% for 5 minutes, promote") and repair conditions (e.g., "if error rate exceeds 5%, roll back").
Cloud Deploy maintains a full audit trail of each release, rollout, and promotion event in Cloud Audit Logs, supporting change management and compliance requirements.

For exam questions, Cloud Deploy is the answer when the requirement mentions "progressive delivery," "canary," "blue-green," or "promotion gates" for GKE or Cloud Run workloads; Cloud Build is the answer for CI (build and test), not CD orchestration.

question.title: Embedded ML and Analytics
question.scenario: A retail chain wants to predict next-quarter demand for 50,000 SKUs directly from their existing BigQuery sales data warehouse, without exporting data or managing ML infrastructure. Business analysts must also build dashboards on the predictions using a familiar BI tool.
question.question-text: Which combination of Google Cloud capabilities allows training a forecasting model on BigQuery data and visualizing predictions without moving data out of BigQuery?

choices.choice: BigQuery ML to train a time-series forecasting model in-place using SQL, and Looker Studio connected to BigQuery to visualize prediction output tables
Export data to Cloud Storage, train a model on Vertex AI Workbench, import predictions back to BigQuery, and connect Tableau to BigQuery
Use Cloud Dataflow to run a streaming ML inference pipeline on historical data and write results to Bigtable for Looker Studio to query
Train a scikit-learn model locally, serialize to ONNX, upload to Vertex AI Model Registry, and batch-predict into a Cloud SQL table for reporting

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Two native GCP tools let analysts stay entirely within BigQuery and a Google-native BI toolâ€”no data export, no infrastructure management, no Python required.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: BigQuery ML (BQML) allows data analysts to create, train, and score ML models using standard SQL statements directly against data in BigQuery, without exporting data or provisioning Vertex AI infrastructure. The ARIMA_PLUS model type is purpose-built for time-series demand forecasting at scale. Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio) natively connects to BigQuery as a data source, enabling analysts to build dashboards on BQML prediction tables. Option B involves unnecessary data movement and infrastructure. Option C uses streaming infrastructure for a batch forecasting problem and Bigtable (a poor fit for analytical dashboards). Option D requires local ML expertise and moves predictions out of BigQuery, adding integration complexity.

ul.li: BQML supports a range of model types: linear/logistic regression, k-means, matrix factorization, XGBoost, TensorFlow model import, and ARIMA_PLUS for time-seriesâ€”all trained and scored with SQL.
The ML.FORECAST function generates future predictions directly in SQL; the ML.EVALUATE function returns model metrics (MAE, RMSE) for quick validation without leaving BigQuery.
Looker Studio's BigQuery connector uses the BigQuery Storage Read API for fast columnar reads, making dashboard queries performant even on large prediction output tables.

For exam scenarios, choose BQML when the driver is "SQL users," "no data movement," or "in-place ML on BigQuery data"; choose Vertex AI when the driver is "custom training containers," "hyperparameter tuning," or "MLOps pipelines."

question.title: Confidential Computing
question.scenario: A pharmaceutical company processes genomic research data in GCP under contracts requiring that the cloud provider cannot access data in memory, even during compute operations. Standard encryption at rest and in transit does not satisfy this contractual obligation.
question.question-text: Which GCP capability protects data while it is actively being processed in memory, preventing the hypervisor and cloud operator from reading it?

choices.choice: Confidential VMs, which use AMD SEV or Intel TDX to encrypt VM memory with a per-VM key that the hypervisor cannot access
Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) via Cloud KMS applied to all persistent disks attached to the VM
VPC Service Controls wrapping the project containing the VMs to prevent data exfiltration
Shielded VMs with Secure Boot and vTPM enabled to verify the integrity of the VM firmware and OS

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the GCP feature that extends encryption to RAM during active computationâ€”not just to disk or networkâ€”using hardware-level memory encryption technology.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Confidential VMs use AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) or Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) to encrypt the VM's memory with encryption keys generated and managed by the AMD/Intel processor, inaccessible to the hypervisor, Google operators, or other VMs on the same host. This satisfies the "data in use" protection requirement. CMEK (Option B) encrypts data at rest on persistent disksâ€”it does not protect data while in RAM during computation. VPC Service Controls (Option C) prevent API-level data movement but do not protect memory. Shielded VMs (Option D) verify the boot chain integrity against rootkits and firmware tampering but do not encrypt memory during processing.

ul.li: Confidential VMs are available for N2D (AMD SEV), C3 (Intel TDX), and select other machine families; enabling them requires selecting the "Confidential VM service" option, which also automatically enables Shielded VM features.

The attestation report generated by the AMD SEV or Intel TDX hardware can be verified by a third party to cryptographically prove that the workload ran inside a genuine confidential enclave, supporting regulatory audit requirements.
Confidential GKE Nodes extend this protection to Kubernetes worker nodes, encrypting memory for all pods running on those nodes with no application code changes required.
Confidential Computing addresses the "data in use" gap in the encryption lifecycle: at rest (CMEK/CSEK), in transit (TLS), and in use (Confidential VMs) together cover all three phases.

question.title: VPC Service Controls Perimeter
question.scenario: A financial institution stores sensitive trading data in BigQuery and Cloud Storage. The security team discovered that a misconfigured IAM binding allowed a service account to copy data to an external project. They need a control that prevents data exfiltration at the API level, regardless of IAM misconfigurations.
question.question-text: Which GCP service creates an API-level security perimeter that prevents data from moving out of approved projects even when IAM permissions would otherwise allow it?

choices.choice: VPC firewall rules with deny-all egress applied to all VMs in the affected projects
Cloud Armor security policies that inspect and block HTTP requests containing sensitive data patterns
Organization Policy constraints that prevent creation of external-facing resources in the affected projects
VPC Service Controls, which wraps a set of projects in a perimeter and blocks API requests that would move data across the perimeter boundary

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The control needed operates at the GCP API call level, not the network packet levelâ€”it blocks copy/read operations that cross a project boundary regardless of who authorized them.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) creates a security perimeter around GCP projects and restricts which service APIs can exchange data across the perimeter boundary. Even if a service account has the IAM permission to copy a BigQuery dataset to an external project, VPC-SC denies the API call if it would move data outside the perimeter. This provides a defense-in-depth layer above IAM. Cloud Armor (Option B) protects against web-layer attacks and inspects HTTP traffic, not GCP API calls. Organization Policy (Option C) restricts resource types and configurations but does not control data movement between projects. VPC firewall rules (Option D) control VM-level network traffic, not API calls from managed services like BigQuery.

ul.li: VPC-SC perimeters enforce access restrictions on over 100 GCP APIs including BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, Spanner, and Cloud KMS; access policies are defined at the organization level.

Access levels (defined via Access Context Manager) allow exceptions to perimeter rules based on device attributes, IP ranges, or user identity, enabling authorized external access without weakening the perimeter for all traffic.
Dry-run mode (audit mode) allows organizations to observe which API calls would be blocked before enforcing the perimeter, reducing the risk of production disruption during rollout.
VPC-SC paired with Cloud DLP creates a two-layer defense: VPC-SC prevents bulk exfiltration at the API level, while DLP detects and redacts sensitive data that passes through approved access paths.

question.title: Cloud Tasks vs Pub/Sub
question.scenario: A logistics platform needs to send HTTP POST requests to a third-party shipping API for each new order. Each request must be delivered exactly once, the rate must be throttled to 100 requests per second to respect the API's rate limit, and failed requests must retry with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours.
question.question-text: Which GCP messaging service is most appropriate for this use case?

choices.choice: Cloud Pub/Sub with a push subscription to the shipping API endpoint and a default retry policy
Cloud Tasks, which allows rate limiting, deduplication, configurable retry schedules, and targets a specific HTTP endpoint or Cloud Run service
Cloud Scheduler triggering a Cloud Function every second to process one order at a time
Cloud Pub/Sub with a pull subscription and a consumer that self-throttles by calling sleep between requests

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need to control the exact dispatch rate to a specific endpoint and get explicit retry scheduling with a long retry window, one service is designed for exactly that.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Tasks is designed for dispatching individual HTTP tasks to specific endpoints with controlled rate limiting (max dispatches per second), configurable retry parameters (max attempts, max retry duration up to 30 days, min/max backoff), and task deduplication via task names. This matches all three requirements: rate throttling to 100 RPS, precise retry scheduling, and targeting a specific third-party HTTP endpoint. Pub/Sub push subscriptions (Option B) do not support rate limiting at the subscription levelâ€”all messages are delivered as fast as possible. Option C uses a polling interval that cannot adapt to variable order volume. Option D requires engineering a self-throttling consumer, adding complexity that Cloud Tasks handles natively.

ul.li: Cloud Tasks supports HTTP targets (any URL) and App Engine targets; the HTTP target type supports authentication via OIDC tokens, enabling secure dispatch to Cloud Run and Cloud Functions without exposing public endpoints without auth.

Task deduplication: if you create a task with the same name within a deduplication window (about 1 hour after task deletion), Cloud Tasks returns the existing task rather than creating a duplicateâ€”useful for idempotent order processing.

Cloud Pub/Sub is the better choice when events are fan-out (multiple subscribers), unordered, or when the producer does not care which consumer handles the message; Cloud Tasks is better when dispatch must be to a specific endpoint with controlled rate and scheduling.
Cloud Tasks queue-level rate limits (maxDispatchesPerSecond, maxConcurrentDispatches, maxBurstSize) allow precise throttling without any application-level rate limiting code in the consumer.

question.title: Vertex AI Training and Serving
question.scenario: A fraud detection team has written a custom TensorFlow model training script. They need to run distributed training jobs on GPU clusters, track experiment metrics, register the trained model, and deploy it to a scalable online prediction endpointâ€”all within a managed ML platform.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides a unified platform for managed training, experiment tracking, model registry, and online serving for custom ML models?

choices.choice: GKE with a custom Kubernetes operator for training jobs, Cloud Storage for model artifacts, and a self-managed TensorFlow Serving deployment
Cloud Dataflow for distributed training, BigQuery ML for model registration, and Cloud Run for serving inference requests
Vertex AI, using Training Custom Jobs for distributed GPU training, Vertex AI Experiments for metric tracking, Model Registry for versioning, and Vertex AI Endpoints for online serving
AI Platform (legacy) Training for distributed jobs and Cloud Functions for prediction serving

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the GCP platform that covers the entire MLOps lifecycleâ€”training, tracking, registration, and servingâ€”under a single product umbrella.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Vertex AI is Google Cloud's unified ML platform, consolidating what was previously AI Platform Training, AI Platform Prediction, and multiple standalone products. Vertex AI Custom Training supports distributed training on CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs using any framework in custom containers. Vertex AI Experiments logs metrics, parameters, and artifacts for each training run. The Vertex AI Model Registry versions trained models with lineage metadata. Vertex AI Endpoints deploys registered models to autoscaling online prediction endpoints with traffic splitting. Option B uses Dataflow (a data pipeline tool, not an ML training platform) and BigQuery ML (SQL-based, not custom model support). Option C is valid architecturally but introduces substantial self-managed operational overhead. Option D references the legacy AI Platform brand, which has been superseded by Vertex AI.

ul.li: Vertex AI Training Custom Jobs support machine learning frameworks via pre-built containers (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn, XGBoost) or fully custom Docker containers pushed to Artifact Registry.
Vertex AI Pipelines (built on KFP or TFX) orchestrate multi-step ML workflows from data preprocessing through training to deployment, enabling reproducible and automated model retraining.
Vertex AI Model Monitoring detects training-serving skew and prediction drift on deployed endpoints by comparing production prediction distributions to a training baseline, alerting on degradation.

For exam scenarios, Vertex AI is always the answer for managed custom ML; BigQuery ML is for SQL-based in-warehouse ML; Dataflow is for data transformation pipelines that feed ML, not for training itself.

question.title: AlloyDB vs Cloud SQL
question.scenario: An enterprise application currently uses PostgreSQL on Cloud SQL. The database team reports that analytical queries on the OLTP database are degrading transaction performance. They need a PostgreSQL-compatible solution that can handle both high-throughput OLTP and complex analytical queries on the same dataset without ETL to a separate warehouse.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud managed PostgreSQL-compatible service is optimized for this hybrid OLTP and analytical workload pattern?

choices.choice: Migrate to Cloud Spanner, which handles both OLTP and analytics through its distributed SQL engine
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with read replicas dedicated to analytical queries, keeping analytical traffic off the primary
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, which uses a disaggregated storage architecture with a columnar engine for analytics and a primary instance for OLTP, both accessing the same underlying data
Keep Cloud SQL for OLTP and add a nightly BigQuery export for analytical queries

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: One Google Cloud database service was specifically designed for PostgreSQL workloads that need both fast transactions and fast analytics on the same data without separate systems.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is Google Cloud's enterprise-grade PostgreSQL-compatible database that uses a disaggregated, log-structured storage layer shared between the primary instance and read pool instances. Its built-in columnar engine automatically materializes hot analytical data in a column-oriented format accessible from the same connection string, enabling analytical queries to run 100x faster than standard PostgreSQL without ETL. Option B with Cloud SQL read replicas still uses row storage on replicas, offering limited analytical performance improvement. Option C migrates to a different database engine (Spanner) requiring application changes and potentially data migration. Option D adds ETL latency and duplicates storage, which the team specifically wanted to avoid.

ul.li: AlloyDB's columnar engine is an adaptive feature that automatically identifies frequently scanned columns and materializes them in a compressed columnar format in memory; it activates with a configuration flag (google_columnar_engine.enabled=on) and requires no schema changes.

AlloyDB uses a shared distributed storage layer (similar to Aurora's approach) where the primary and read pool instances all access the same storage, enabling sub-second replication lag to read pool nodes.
AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, containerized version of AlloyDB that runs on-premises or in other clouds, enabling hybrid deployments where some data must stay on-premises.

Distinguish for the exam: Cloud SQL = standard managed PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server, best for existing workloads; AlloyDB = high-performance PostgreSQL for demanding OLTP + analytics; Spanner = horizontally scalable, globally distributed, non-PostgreSQL wire protocol (though has PostgreSQL interface).

question.title: Private DNS and Split-Horizon
question.scenario: A hybrid enterprise runs workloads in GCP and on-premises. Internal services use the same hostnames in both environments (e.g., api.internal.corp.com), but GCP instances must resolve to private IP addresses in the VPC while on-premises systems resolve to on-premises IPs. External DNS must not expose internal hostnames.
question.question-text: Which Cloud DNS configuration pattern implements this split-horizon DNS requirement?

choices.choice: Create a Cloud DNS public zone for internal.corp.com and restrict access using Cloud Armor IP allowlisting
Create a Cloud DNS private zone for internal.corp.com visible only to specified VPC networks, with records pointing to GCP internal IPs, while the public zone remains on the corporate DNS server
Use Cloud DNS forwarding zones to send all DNS queries to the on-premises resolver, which returns GCP internal IPs for GCP resources
Configure split-horizon using VPC firewall rules that block DNS port 53 traffic from external IP ranges

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud DNS private zones are visible only to VMs within associated VPC networksâ€”they are invisible to the public internet by design, making them the natural split-horizon tool.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A Cloud DNS private zone is only resolvable from within the VPC networks explicitly associated with it. Creating a private zone for internal.corp.com with records pointing to GCP private IPs means GCP VMs resolve the hostnames to internal addresses, while the same hostnames on the public internet (or on-premises) resolve through the corporate DNS infrastructure to different addresses. This is the canonical split-horizon pattern. Option B makes internal hostnames publicly resolvable, violating the requirement. Option C creates a dependency on the on-premises resolver for all GCP DNS resolution, creating latency and an availability dependency. Option D misuses firewall rules to solve a DNS routing problem; firewalls don't change what DNS records are returned.

ul.li: Cloud DNS private zones can be associated with multiple VPC networks, including those in different projects via Shared VPC or peered VPCs, enabling consistent internal hostname resolution across an organization's network topology.

DNS peering (Cloud DNS to Cloud DNS) allows a VPC to delegate resolution of a subdomain to another VPC's private zoneâ€”useful when a hub VPC owns the DNS zone and spoke VPCs need to resolve names from it.

Inbound and outbound DNS forwarding via a Cloud DNS forwarding zone and a Cloud DNS server policy enable hybrid resolution: GCP VMs can query on-premises resolvers for on-premises zones, and on-premises hosts can query Cloud DNS via the inbound DNS forwarding IP in the VPC.
The Google-provided internal DNS automatically creates FQDN records in the format INSTANCE.ZONE.c.PROJECT_ID.internal for every VM; custom hostnames require explicit private zone records.

question.title: VM Patch Compliance
question.scenario: A company runs 800 Compute Engine VMs across multiple projects. The security team requires centralized visibility into OS patch status, the ability to schedule automated patching during maintenance windows, and compliance reports showing which VMs are out of date without installing third-party agents.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides centralized, agent-based OS patch management and compliance reporting for Compute Engine VMs at scale?

choices.choice: Cloud Build pipelines that bake updated OS images and replace VMs using a rolling Managed Instance Group update
Cloud Scheduler triggering a Cloud Function that SSH-es into each VM and runs apt-get upgrade or yum update
VM Manager (OS Config), which uses the OS Config agent pre-installed on GCP VMs to enforce patch policies, schedule patch jobs, and report patch compliance across projects
Security Command Center's vulnerability scanning feature, which patches VMs automatically when it detects outdated packages

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP ships a lightweight OS Config agent with its public images and wraps it in a managed service for patch orchestrationâ€”no third-party tools needed.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VM Manager (OS Config) is Google Cloud's managed OS configuration and patch service. The OS Config agent ships pre-installed in GCP public OS images and can be deployed to custom images. VM Manager's Patch Management feature allows creating patch jobs that target VMs by zone, label, or resource group, scheduling them within maintenance windows, and tracking compliance in a centralized dashboard across projects. It supports Windows Update and Linux package managers (apt, yum, zypper) natively. Option B requires SSH access and custom scripting, which doesn't scale to 800 VMs and creates security exposure. Option C involves image replacement (immutable infra pattern), which is different from in-place patching and may not be appropriate for all VMs. Option D misattributes automatic patching to SCC, which provides vulnerability findings but does not apply patches.

ul.li: VM Manager OS Policies allow declarative specification of desired OS state (packages installed, files present, services running) and continuously report drift, functioning as a lightweight configuration management tool without Chef or Puppet.
Patch compliance reports aggregate per-VM patch state (up-to-date, pending, failed) and can be exported to BigQuery via a log sink for long-term trending and SLA reporting.
Patch rollout strategies in VM Manager support canary-style deployments: patch a percentage of VMs first, then proceed to the rest, limiting blast radius if a patch causes issues.

For exam scenarios, VM Manager/OS Config is the answer for GCP-native in-place patch management; Managed Instance Group rolling updates address immutable infrastructure replacement; these are complementary, not competing, patterns.

question.title: Capacity Planning with Metrics
question.scenario: An SRE team manages a GKE cluster running a stateful application. They want to receive alerts when CPU utilization across all nodes exceeds 80% for 10 consecutive minutes, and they want to build a dashboard showing historical CPU trends to inform capacity planning decisions.
question.question-text: Which GCP observability tooling correctly implements both the alerting and the historical trending requirements?

choices.choice: Cloud Monitoring alert policies using the kubernetes.io/node/cpu/allocatable_utilization metric with a 10-minute alignment window, and a Cloud Monitoring dashboard with a line chart widget for the same metric
Cloud Logging log-based metrics that parse kubelet logs for CPU usage, with Log-based alert policies and a Logs Explorer saved query for trending
Cloud Trace latency percentile dashboards as a proxy for CPU load, with alert policies on p99 latency thresholds
A Cloud Scheduler job that calls the Monitoring API every 10 minutes, stores results in Firestore, and triggers a Cloud Function alert if the threshold is crossed

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Monitoring collects GKE infrastructure metrics automatically and provides both alerting policies and dashboard widgets nativelyâ€”no custom polling or log parsing needed.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Monitoring automatically ingests GKE node and workload metrics from the GKE system metrics pipeline. Alert policies can target any metric with conditions specifying alignment period, aggregation, and threshold; a 10-minute window with the kubernetes.io/node/cpu/allocatable_utilization metric across the cluster directly satisfies the requirement. Cloud Monitoring dashboards with chart widgets plot the same metrics over configurable time ranges (hours to months) for capacity planning analysis. Option B uses log-based metrics for something that is already a first-class metricâ€”inefficient and imprecise. Option C uses latency as a CPU proxy, which is indirect and unreliable. Option D reinvents Cloud Monitoring with significant engineering overhead.

ul.li: Cloud Monitoring Managed Service for Prometheus (GMP) collects workload-level metrics from pods using the Prometheus exposition format, complementing the GKE infrastructure metrics for application-level capacity planning.

Alert policy conditions support multiple aggregation functions (mean, percentile, sum) and cross-series reducers (mean across all nodes in a cluster), enabling cluster-wide thresholds rather than per-node alerts.

Cloud Monitoring retains metrics data for 6 weeks by default; for longer-term capacity planning, exporting metrics to BigQuery via a Metrics Export (beta) or using Monitoring API queries against historical data points is necessary.

Uptime checks and SLO monitoring in Cloud Monitoring complement alerting by providing user-facing availability signals that correlate with infrastructure capacity signals in the same dashboarding environment.

question.title: Artifact Registry Migration
question.scenario: A platform engineering team stores Docker images in Container Registry (gcr.io). Google has announced Container Registry is deprecated. The team needs to migrate to the supported replacement, which must also support non-Docker artifact formats like Helm charts and Maven packages in the same service.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service is the official replacement for Container Registry and supports multi-format artifact storage?

choices.choice: Cloud Storage buckets with a custom Nginx proxy providing the Docker registry V2 API
Artifact Registry, which supports Docker images, Helm charts, Maven, npm, Python, and other package formats in regionally scoped repositories with fine-grained IAM
GitHub Packages integrated with Cloud Build via a secret stored in Secret Manager
GKE's built-in registry that caches images locally on each node pool for faster pulls

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google officially deprecated Container Registry in favor of a single service that handles all artifact formats, not just Docker images.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Artifact Registry is the official successor to Container Registry. It provides dedicated repositories per format (Docker, Helm, Maven, npm, Python, APT, YUM, and more) in a single service, with repositories scoped to a region for data residency control. IAM permissions are applied at the repository level, enabling fine-grained access control. It integrates natively with Cloud Build, GKE, and Cloud Run for image pulls, and supports vulnerability scanning via Artifact Analysis. Option B is a custom engineering solution that provides Docker registry functionality only. Option C introduces an external dependency on GitHub. Option D describes node image caching (Image Streaming), not a registry service.

ul.li: Container Registry gcr.io domains are backed by Cloud Storage buckets; Artifact Registry uses its own storage backend and the migration tool (gcloud artifacts docker upgrade migrate) can migrate images while preserving tags.

Artifact Registry supports virtual repositories that aggregate multiple upstream repositories (including npm Registry, PyPI, Maven Central) as a proxy with caching, reducing dependency on external networks and enabling a private dependency mirror.

Artifact Registry's Artifact Analysis service runs on-push vulnerability scanning for OS packages and language dependencies (Java, Go, Node.js, Python) in container images, generating SBOM data and CVE reports accessible via the containeranalysis API.

For exam questions, if asked about "artifact storage" or "container registry replacement," the answer is always Artifact Registry; if asked about "image caching on nodes," the answer is GKE Image Streaming or node-level containerd caching.

question.title: Scheduled Job Management
question.scenario: A data engineering team needs to trigger a Cloud Run data ingestion job every day at 2:00 AM UTC, a BigQuery data export every Monday at 6:00 AM UTC, and a weekly cleanup Cloud Function every Sunday at midnight. They want a single managed service to own all three schedules without running cron on a VM.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service is designed to execute cron-based schedules that invoke Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, Pub/Sub, or arbitrary HTTP endpoints?

choices.choice: Cloud Workflows with a timed wait step that re-executes the workflow on a recurring cadence
Cloud Tasks with a scheduled delivery time set per task by the ingestion pipeline itself
Cloud Scheduler, which manages cron-syntax schedules and dispatches HTTP, Pub/Sub, or App Engine HTTP targets at the configured time
Eventarc with a Cloud Pub/Sub scheduled message producer that simulates cron firing

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP has a purpose-built, fully managed cron scheduler that accepts standard unix cron syntax and targets HTTP endpoints or Pub/Sub topicsâ€”no VMs, no custom code.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Scheduler is Google Cloud's fully managed cron job service. Jobs are defined with a unix-cron or App Engine cron syntax schedule, a timezone, and a target (HTTP/HTTPS URL, Pub/Sub topic, or App Engine HTTP). It dispatches an HTTP POST to a Cloud Run URL or publishes a Pub/Sub message at the scheduled time, triggering any downstream Cloud Function or workflow. It handles retries automatically if the target returns an error. Option B uses Cloud Tasks for one-time future delivery, not recurring schedules. Option C with Cloud Workflows can be made to recur but requires engineering a self-re-scheduling pattern, adding complexity. Option D requires a custom Pub/Sub message producer, negating the managed-service benefit.

ul.li: Cloud Scheduler jobs support IANA timezone names (e.g., America/Los_Angeles), enabling schedules defined in local business time rather than UTC, automatically adjusting for DST.

Cloud Scheduler uses OIDC or OAuth2 tokens on HTTP targets to authenticate to protected Cloud Run or Cloud Functions endpoints, eliminating the need to expose unauthenticated endpoints for scheduled invocations.
Cloud Scheduler integrates with Cloud Monitoring and emits metrics for job execution count and status, enabling alerts if a scheduled job fails or does not execute within the expected window.

For exam questions, Cloud Scheduler = recurring time-based triggers; Cloud Tasks = future one-time or retried task dispatch; Cloud Workflows = multi-step orchestration with conditional logic; these are complementary and often used together.

question.title: Resource Hierarchy Governance
question.scenario: A large enterprise is migrating 50 business units to GCP. Each unit needs its own GCP projects but must comply with corporate-wide policies (e.g., no public Cloud Storage buckets, compute resources only in approved regions). Individual teams must not be able to override these constraints in their projects.
question.question-text: Which GCP Resource Manager concept allows the enterprise to apply hierarchical, inheritable governance policies that individual teams cannot override?

choices.choice: Billing budget alerts that notify security when a project creates non-compliant resources
IAM deny policies applied to each project individually, listing every restricted action for each team member
VPC firewall rules at the VPC level that prevent non-compliant resource creation
Organization Policy Service constraints applied at the organization or folder level, which are inherited by all descendant projects and cannot be weakened by child nodes

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The GCP resource hierarchy (organization â†’ folders â†’ projects) supports policy inheritance, and one service enforces configuration constraints that flow down the hierarchy with no override possible at child levels.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Organization Policy Service allows administrators to set constraintsâ€”such as constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention or constraints/gcp.resourceLocationsâ€”at the organization or folder level. These constraints are enforced by GCP APIs: if a project tries to create a public Cloud Storage bucket and the publicAccessPrevention constraint is enforced at the organization level, the API call is rejected regardless of the project-level settings or the caller's IAM permissions. Policy inheritance flows from parent to child, and child nodes can only restrict, not relax, inherited constraints. Option B requires per-project IAM deny configuration and doesn't scale to 50 business units. Option C uses firewall rules for network traffic, not resource configuration enforcement. Option D is detective, not preventiveâ€”it alerts after the fact.

ul.li: Organization Policy constraints come in two types: list constraints (allow/deny specific values, e.g., allowed VM images) and boolean constraints (enforce or not enforce a binary policy, e.g., disableServiceAccountCreation).

Folders in the resource hierarchy group related projects (e.g., per-business-unit or per-environment folders) and allow different policy configurations at each folder level, enabling fine-grained governance without a flat project namespace.

Custom Organization Policy constraints (generally available) allow enterprises to write CEL-based policies against any GCP resource field, extending beyond the built-in constraint catalog to organization-specific governance rules.
Policy tags in Data Catalog complement Organization Policy by governing access to specific BigQuery columns, providing data-level governance in addition to resource-level governance.

question.title: GKE Autopilot vs Standard
question.scenario: A startup wants to run containerized microservices on GKE. Their platform engineer has limited Kubernetes expertise and wants to minimize node management, capacity planning, and OS patching overhead. The team is cost-conscious and wants to pay only for the vCPU and memory requested by their pods, not for idle node capacity.
question.question-text: Which GKE mode of operation eliminates node pool management and charges only for requested pod resources?

choices.choice: GKE Standard with Cluster Autoscaler enabled, which adds and removes nodes based on pending pod demand
GKE Autopilot, which manages node provisioning, scaling, and patching automatically and bills per pod based on requested vCPU, memory, and ephemeral storage
GKE Standard with Preemptible node pools to minimize cost and manual node resizing based on utilization metrics
Cloud Run for Anthos, which runs containers on GKE nodes but abstracts Kubernetes manifests entirely

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: One GKE mode removes all node-level responsibilities from the operator and changes the billing unit from node hours to pod-requested resources.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: GKE Autopilot is a managed Kubernetes mode where Google owns and operates the node infrastructure: it provisions, scales, patches, and secures nodes automatically. Customers interact only with Kubernetes workload resources (Deployments, Services, etc.) and are billed for the vCPU, memory, and ephemeral storage requested in pod specsâ€”not for node capacity that may be idle. This directly addresses the team's limited Kubernetes expertise and pay-for-use cost model. GKE Standard with Cluster Autoscaler (Option B) still requires operators to manage node pools, machine types, and OS updates. Option C with Preemptible nodes reduces cost but increases operational complexity. Option D (Cloud Run for Anthos, now called Cloud Run on GKE) is a different product for serving HTTP workloads and does not generalize to arbitrary containerized microservices.

ul.li: GKE Autopilot enforces security best practices by default: nodes run with Container-Optimized OS, Workload Identity is mandatory, privilege escalation in pods is blocked, and host-path volumes are disallowedâ€”these restrictions cannot be overridden.

Autopilot billing is per-second for pod-requested resources with a minimum of 10 minutes; idle nodes do not accrue charges, which makes it cost-efficient for workloads with variable or low average utilization.
GKE Autopilot supports Spot Pods (analogous to Preemptible VMs) which reduce pod-resource pricing by up to 60% for interruption-tolerant batch workloads.

For exam scenarios, choose Autopilot when the requirements emphasize reduced operational overhead, no node management, or pod-level billing; choose Standard when requirements include DaemonSets, custom node images, specific hardware (GPUs, TPUs), or workloads that need privileged containers.

question.title: Sensitive Data Classification
question.scenario: A healthcare company wants to scan Cloud Storage buckets and BigQuery tables across their organization for patient names, Social Security Numbers, and credit card numbers. Discovered sensitive data must be classified and reported, and certain fields in BigQuery must be automatically de-identified before analysts can query them.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides automated discovery, classification, and de-identification of sensitive data across Cloud Storage and BigQuery?

choices.choice: BigQuery column-level security with policy tags applied to columns labeled as sensitive after a manual review process
Security Command Center Premium with sensitive data findings enabled in the Sensitive Data Protection category

Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP), which scans data using 150+ built-in and custom infoTypes, classifies findings by sensitivity, and can de-identify data using masking, tokenization, or encryption transformations
Cloud Healthcare API's de-identification feature, which is limited to FHIR and DICOM resources in the Healthcare API

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The GCP service designed specifically for sensitive data discovery, classification, and transformation across storage services is the one whose name explicitly references data loss prevention.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud DLP (now called Sensitive Data Protection) is the purpose-built service for sensitive data management. It can run inspection jobs against Cloud Storage files and BigQuery tables using over 150 built-in infoType detectors for PII, PHI, financial data, and credentials, plus custom regex or dictionary patterns. Discovery jobs automatically scan entire organizations. Classification results are tagged and can be sent to Security Command Center or BigQuery for reporting. De-identification jobs transform data using masking, hashing, tokenization, format-preserving encryption, or date shifting without changing table schemas. Option B uses SCC as a consumer of Cloud DLP findings, not as the scanning engine itself. Option C requires manual review and only controls accessâ€”it doesn't discover or de-identify. Option D is limited to a specific data format and API.

ul.li: Cloud DLP infoType detectors use pattern matching, context clues, and machine learning to maximize precision; for example, SSN detection considers surrounding context (e.g., "SSN:" prefix) to reduce false positives from strings that happen to match the format.

The de-identification transformation CryptoReplaceFfxFpeConfig performs format-preserving encryption, producing a ciphertext that maintains the same format and length as the original (e.g., a 16-digit number for a credit card), enabling analytics on de-identified data that requires the original format.

Automatic discovery in Sensitive Data Protection (the new product name for Cloud DLP) continuously monitors newly created BigQuery tables and Cloud Storage objects, generating data profiles that summarize the risk level of each asset.

Policy tags in BigQuery Data Catalog integrate with Cloud DLP: when DLP scans classify a column as containing sensitive data, policy tags can be automatically applied to enforce column-level access control going forward.

question.title: Context-Aware Access Control
question.scenario: A company allows employees to access Google Cloud Console and internal web applications from personal devices. The security team wants to restrict access to sensitive GCP resources so that only requests originating from managed corporate devices with up-to-date OS versions are allowed, without requiring a VPN.
question.question-text: Which GCP service enforces device-posture and context-based conditions on access to GCP resources and Google Workspace applications?

choices.choice: Binary Authorization policies that verify device certificates before allowing API calls
Cloud Armor security policies with custom rules that inspect HTTP headers for device management tokens
Access Context Manager, which defines access levels based on device attributes, IP ranges, and user identity, and applies them to resources via VPC Service Controls and Identity-Aware Proxy
VPN gateway with certificate-based authentication that only corporate managed-device certificates can complete

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The GCP service that defines access levels based on device posture and applies them as additional conditions on resource access is part of Google's BeyondCorp zero-trust framework.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Access Context Manager is the GCP component that enables BeyondCorp Enterprise zero-trust access policies. Access levels define conditions such as device management status (enrolled in endpoint verification), OS version, IP address range, and user identity. These access levels are applied to resource access in two ways: as conditions in VPC Service Controls perimeters (blocking API calls from non-compliant contexts) and as IAM conditions or Identity-Aware Proxy policies (blocking web application access). This enables context-aware access without VPN. Cloud Armor (Option B) operates at the HTTP layer but cannot evaluate device management posture. Binary Authorization (Option C) enforces container image signing, not device access control. Option D requires VPN infrastructure, which the requirement explicitly excludes.

ul.li: Access Context Manager access levels support BASIC and CUSTOM (CEL-based) condition types; CUSTOM levels allow complex expressions combining device attributes, user identity, and request time to define fine-grained access conditions.

Endpoint Verification, a Chrome extension and Google endpoint management integration, collects device attributes (OS version, disk encryption status, screen lock) and makes them available to Access Context Manager for evaluation.

Access levels are applied within an access policy (organization-scoped) and can be reused across multiple VPC Service Controls perimeters and IAP-protected resources, enabling consistent posture-based policies across the entire GCP organization.

For exam questions, BeyondCorp/zero-trust access maps to Identity-Aware Proxy + Access Context Manager; perimeter-based data protection maps to VPC Service Controls; these are complementary layers of the same zero-trust architecture.

question.title: Managed vs Self-Managed Trade-offs
question.scenario: A startup architect is choosing between running a self-managed PostgreSQL database on Compute Engine VMs and using Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The team of three engineers must also maintain the rest of the application infrastructure. The CEO wants a cost comparison that accounts for total cost of ownership, not just instance pricing.
question.question-text: Which factors make managed services like Cloud SQL typically lower in total cost of ownership than self-managed equivalents on GCE VMs, even if the hourly rate appears higher?

choices.choice: Managed services always have lower compute costs because Google achieves greater hardware utilization than customers running their own VMs

Managed services eliminate or reduce labor costs for patching, backup, HA configuration, failover testing, and monitoring setup, which for a small team often exceeds the price premium of the managed service
Managed services avoid egress charges entirely because data stays within Google's network, while self-managed VMs incur egress costs on all database traffic
Managed services offer unlimited storage at no additional charge, eliminating the storage cost component of TCO that self-managed solutions incur

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The true cost of any service includes not just infrastructure pricing but also the engineering time required to build, operate, and maintain itâ€”especially for a small team.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Total cost of ownership for self-managed databases on VMs includes: database software licensing or configuration, OS patching and hardening, backup scheduling and restoration testing, HA setup (Patroni, Pacemaker, or manual replication), failover testing, monitoring and alerting configuration, and on-call burden for incidents. For a three-engineer team, these operational tasks represent a significant fraction of engineering capacityâ€”often more costly than the Cloud SQL price premium. Cloud SQL provides automated backups, point-in-time recovery, HA with automatic failover, read replicas, integrated Cloud Monitoring metrics, and maintenance patchingâ€”all included. Options B, C, and D contain false or overstated claims: managed services are not always cheaper on compute, egress costs apply to both equally for external traffic, and managed storage is priced per GB like any other storage.

ul.li: The "ops tax" on self-managed infrastructure is nonlinear: a team of 3 engineers spending 20% of their time on database operations is effectively losing 0.6 FTE, which at loaded engineering cost rates often exceeds thousands of dollars per monthâ€”far more than the Cloud SQL premium over raw GCE costs.

Managed service SLAs (Cloud SQL's 99.95% for HA instances) transfer downtime risk to Google; a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster requires engineering effort to achieve and maintain comparable availability, including runbook development and failover drills.

Scale-up vs. scale-out decisions are another TCO factor: Cloud SQL instances can be resized with a maintenance window, while self-managed clusters may require data migration, schema changes, or application changes to scale horizontally.

For architecture trade-off exam questions, the correct framing is always: managed services trade higher unit cost for lower operational complexity; the decision depends on team size, expertise, and the opportunity cost of engineering timeâ€”not on raw instance pricing alone.
